title: From Cellular Stress to Systemic Adaptation: The Circadian Clock and Stress Response at Cellular and Systemic Levels
content: The stress response is essential for cellular and organismal survival as it acts as a protective and adaptive mechanism to maintain homeostasis. At the organismal level, animal stress response is mediated by glucocorticoids. In mammals, these steroid hormones are secreted under the control of the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal (HPA) axis and regulate systemic changes under stressful conditions. At the cellular level, cellular stressors are sensed by four protein kinases of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2α (eIF2α) and activate the evolutionarily conserved integrated stress response (ISR), which converges on phosphorylation of Serine 51 on eIF2α. Prolonged stress is energy consuming and detrimental to the health of cells and animals, and the magnitude and timing of stress is intricately controlled by the circadian timing system. Recent studies have found a number of crosstalk mechanisms between HPA, ISR, and the circadian clock. To summarize these recent advances, the review introduces the architecture of the circadian system, the HPA axis and ISR, and the bidirectional relationship between stress and the circadian system in physiology and diseases. Understanding the interactions between stress and the circadian clock will provide new insight into disease mechanisms and may inform chronotherapeutic strategies to restore temporal homeostasis.
